sweep_summary: Eleven title hits for Sanskrit (sans1269; catalog = tonal, deciding source Whitney 1889 §§80-96, corroborated by Burrow 1955 and, from our earlier reading, Macdonell 1910/1916, Wackernagel 1896, Kiparsky 2010). Two items were obtained open and read: Bender 1915 (IF 34, archive.org whole-volume scanned) — a corpus count of udātta placement in -mant/-vant derivatives (accent stays on the base except after final-accented i/u/r/-an stems), refining the placement note, silent on pitch vs stress; and Perry & Vaux 2018 (accepted manuscript on Cambridge Apollo) — pitch-mark description (udātta/svarita/sannatara) plus the Kiparsky-Halle Basic Accentual Principle (leftmost underlying accent, else initial), refining placement in the same way as Kiparsky 2010 and consistent with the tonal coding. A Crossref title search also surfaced an open-access 2026 paper not in the target list, Ryan, 'The role of pitch accent in Vedic Sanskrit poetics' (Phonological Data and Analysis 8, CC-BY), downloaded and read: one accent per word, any syllable, 'tone, not stress', with Rigveda-wide statistics showing the accent is inert in meter — the best new first-hand statement; it confirms rather than supersedes Whitney. Of the rest: Allen 1951 (BSOAS) is Firthian prosody of retroflexion/aspiration (first-page excerpt seen; irrelevant); Mair & Mei 1991 (HJAS/JSTOR) is verse prosody, not word accent (title/Crossref only); Selkirk 1980 (two duplicate Glottolog records; Aronoff & Kean are editors, not co-authors) is prosodic domains/sandhi, no open copy; Janda & Joseph 2002 (De Gruyter, bot-blocked) likely a prosodic-domain critique, unclear and low priority; Katre 1978 (De Gruyter, paywalled; festschrift vol. 3 not on archive.org) on Pāṇini's accent rules, low priority; Kulikov 1997 (print festschrift, no open copy) a note on an accent shift in one verb class, low; Levin 1971 (SUNY Press; archive.org lending-restricted only) comparative, low; Calabrese & Grestenberger 2023 is an unpublished manuscript (Glottolog 'Ms.'), not on LingBuzz or Calabrese's site, medium priority as a modern morphophonological placement analysis. Glottolog author lists for 593927 and 604712 wrongly fold volume editors into the author field. Nothing read contradicts the catalog's tonal coding.

new_statements.quote: In terms of prosodic typology, Vedic is what is commonly known as a pitch accent language, but given that its accent was arguably purely tonal (see below), it could also be called a restricted tone system ... Although I will continue to use the term accent, its phonetic realization should be understood to be tone, not stress. ... Each Vedic word has exactly one accent, with certain well-known exceptions: vocatives, main-clause finite verbs, and certain clitics are unaccented ... Accent is not restricted to a window like it is in, say, Ancient Greek. It can (and frequently does) occur on any syllable of the word, regardless of length.

new_statements.quote: As a general rule, every Vedic word is both accented and has one main accent only. The Udatta is the only main accent in the original text of the Rgveda. It is generally found on the syllable which, according to the evidence of Comparative Philology, bore it in the Indo-European period. [§85, p. 80] — The Vedic accent, like that of ancient Greece, was of an essentially musical nature. This is indicated by the fact that the accent exercises no influence on the rhythm of versification. [§83, p. 77] — The Vedic accent, like the Greek, was, after the beginning of our era, changed to a stress accent which ... is regulated by the quantity of the last two or three syllables, much as in Latin [p. 77 n. 2]

Adds two points the catalog record lacks: the accent had some stress component (p. 77), and the later, post-Vedic pronunciation switched to a weight-regulated stress (p. 77 n. 2).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Vedic Sanskrit has a musical (pitch) accent, the udatta, one main accent per word; its position is not derivable from syllable count or weight but is inherited (lexical, free), and it has no effect on metre. Macdonell adds that it was 'accompanied by some stress' (p. 77) and that after the beginning of our era it was replaced by a Latin-like stress governed by the weight of the last two or three syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §84 d (p. 80): in the Satapatha Brahmana reduplicated forms or long compounds accented on the first syllable or prior member 'sometimes receive a secondary accent near the end of the word' (bálbalīti, éka-catvarimsát); §85 a: infinitives in -tavai and dvandva-type compounds (mitrá-váruna, bŕhas-páti-) carry a double accent.
new_statements.exceptions: §85 b: some words are invariably enclitic (pronouns tva-, sama-, ena-, me, ma, nau, nas, te, tva, vam, vas, im, sim; particles ca, u, va, iva, kam, gha/ha, cid, bhala, smaha, sma, svid) and others lose their accent under sentence conditions (vocative and finite verb of a principal clause, §§93 ff.). Footnote 3 p. 80: the udatta shifted to other syllables in a few words in the Brahmanas and in Panini (saptá > sápta, astáu > ástau).

new_statements.quote: Akzent. Die alte Akzentweise des Sanskrit ist in der heutigen Aussprache nicht mehr gebräuchlich. Jetzige Akzentuation: Die für das Lateinische geltende Akzentregel wird auf die letzten vier Silben ausgedehnt. Der Akzent kann bis zur viertletzten Silbe zurückgehen, vorausgesetzt, daß die vorletzte und drittletzte Silbe kurz sind. Die Länge der vorletzten oder der drittvorletzten zieht den Ton auf sich: dúhitaram (die Tochter), bhávati (er wird), bhavā́mi (ich werde), bhavánti (sie werden). Anm. Bei einfachen Verben wird die Wurzelsilbe betont; Augment, Reduplikation und Verbalpräfix erhalten den Ton, stets unter Einhaltung des Hauptgesetzes.
new_statements.translation: Accent. The old accentuation of Sanskrit is no longer used in present-day pronunciation. Present accentuation: the accent rule that holds for Latin is extended to the last four syllables. The accent can go back as far as the fourth syllable from the end, provided that the penultimate and antepenultimate syllables are short. Length of the penultimate or of the antepenultimate draws the accent onto itself: dúhitaram 'the daughter', bhávati 'he becomes', bhavā́mi 'I become', bhavánti 'they become'. Note. In simple verbs the root syllable is accented; augment, reduplication and verbal prefix receive the accent, always in observance of the main law.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Classical Sanskrit in today's (recitation) pronunciation: a Latin-type weight rule extended to a four-syllable window; a heavy penult takes the stress, else a heavy antepenult, else the stress goes back to the fourth syllable from the end. Morphological tendencies within that window: root syllable in simple verbs; augment, reduplication and preverb take the stress; nominal derivatives usually keep the base's accent. Clusters with y and v do not make position (do not count as heavy) for this rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Consonant groups with y and v do not create length by position for this rule; derivatives of nouns mostly keep the accent of the base word. The old (Vedic) accent system is explicitly declared not in use, and the book confines itself to Classical Sanskrit (preface).

tone_statements.citation: Whitney, William D. 1869. On the Nature and Designation of the Accent in Sanskrit. Transactions of the American Philological Association (1869-70) 1: 20-45.
tone_statements.quote: This suggestion is made a certainty by the names and defi- nitions of the separate accents or " tones." Of these, three are recognized, and they are called respectively uddtta, anu- ddtla, and svarita. Uddtta (passive participle of the root da, with the preposi- tions ut and a~) means literally ' taken up, raised, elevated.' And the description of the accent by all the authorities corres- ponds with this title ; it is defined everywhere, in nearly iden- tical terms, as being utterance uccdis, ' in a high tone.' [...] Anuddtta is the same word with the negative prefix, and so means ' not elevated.' The authorities define it as signifying utterance nicdis, 'in a low tone.' [...] This lowness of tone does not imply, of course, a fall from the ordinary pitch of voice ; the tone is low as compared with uddtta ; it is the simple negation of that uplifting of pitch whiclvmarks the positively accented syllable. The name of the third tone is svarita, and it is uniformly explained as consisting in a combination of the other two.
tone_statements.locator: p. 23; Greek acute/grave/circumflex equivalence p. 25; rules for the svarita/circumflex pp. 26ff.
tone_statements.summary: Pitch accent: one raised (high-pitch) syllable per accented word; following syllable a falling (circumflex-like) svarita; remaining syllables low.

tone_statements.citation: Whitney, William D. 1855 [vol. 5, 1855-56; paper read October 8, 1856]. Contributions from the Atharva-Veda to the Theory of Sanskrit Verbal Accent. Journal of the American Oriental Society 5: 385-419.
tone_statements.quote: The first and most general rule for the accentuation of the verb in the Sanskrit sentence is this. In a direct or inde- pendent sentence, or clause of a sentence, the finite verb is made enclitic upon any word preceding it which is directly connected with it in construction. [...] It is well known that, by the operation of this rule, the Sanskrit verb is in a large majority of cases deprived of its accent. [...] If, however, the verb stands at the head of the sentence, it cannot, of course, be encliticized, but retains its accent
tone_statements.summary: Culminative word accent; finite verb unaccented in main clauses unless initial, accented in subordinate clauses.

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts another once the period is fixed, but the sources split by stage: Macdonell 1910 (Vedic Grammar) and the existing Ryan 2026 statement describe Vedic Sanskrit, with a culminative musical/pitch accent (udatta) whose position is inherited and free and which does not affect metre (Macdonell allows 'some stress' alongside the pitch). Macdonell 1927 §15.10 and Stenzler 1915 §13 describe Classical Sanskrit in its post-Vedic and present-day pronunciation: a Latin-type weight-sensitive stress in a four-syllable window (heavy penult; else antepenult; else fourth from the end), and both say the old accent is no longer used. Macdonell 1910 p. 77 n. 2 itself records the change from the one system to the other. The catalog's single 'Sanskrit' record (rule empty, qs-tier source) plus the Ryan 2026 statement therefore cover only the Vedic stage; a Classical/modern-pronunciation entry would be weight-sensitive. Bopp 1854 vol. I is silent; Lubotsky 1988 and Levin 1971 could not be opened.

sources.quote: The Vedic texts do not record accent as such. Rather, in manuscripts and critical editions, various pitch features are indicated, from which the placement of the accent can be deduced ... a fall in pitch, known as svarita ('sounded'), and which generally follows the accented syllable, is indicated through a short vertical line above the syllable in question, and a low pitch before the accented syllable, known as sannatara ('more depressed'), is indicated with a horizontal line below the syllable. ... The high-pitched, accented syllable (known as udātta 'raised') is not marked [p. 270]. (7) Basic Accentual Principle (BAP) (as originally formulated by Kiparsky and Halle 1977: 209): If a word has more than one [underlyingly] accented vowel, the first of these gets the word accent. If a word has no [underlyingly] accented vowel, the first vowel gets the word accent. [p. 273]

sources.quote: The first and most general rule for the accentuation of the verb in the Sanskrit sentence is this. In a direct or inde- pendent sentence, or clause of a sentence, the finite verb is made enclitic upon any word preceding it which is directly connected with it in construction. [...] It is well known that, by the operation of this rule, the Sanskrit verb is in a large majority of cases deprived of its accent. [...] If, however, the verb stands at the head of the sentence, it cannot, of course, be encliticized, but retains its accent
sources.note: States and tests the rules for when the finite verb keeps or loses its (pitch) accent: in an independent clause the verb is enclitic (accentless) after any preceding word construed with it (e.g. forms of kr in AV: 498 occurrences, 146 accented, 352 accentless); clause-initial verbs keep the accent; in dependent (ya-, relative/subordinate) clauses the verb retains its proper accent, even at the cost of the accent of a prefixed preposition; the rest of the paper treats antithesis, conditional and other special clause types and corrects the accentuation of the edited AV text.
